This may seem a slightly unusual choice, as it's fan fiction. It is, however, fan fiction of the very highest order: "Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality" by Eliezer Yudkowsky. This is available here. I think it's one of the first important books to be published originally in electronic format.

Most fan fiction is entertaining, but not much of it is serious - that is, most fan fiction doesn't investigate important philosophical ideas through fiction. HPMOR is significant because it attempts to discuss serious matters in an accessible way, whilst managing to include several really good jokes. It gets a bit more serious towards the end, but it remains one of the best expressions of the modern humanist impulse in recent fiction. Eliezer Yudkowsky deserves all the plaudits he has received, and JK Rowling deserves much respect for having the courage to let fan fiction flourish under her aegis. As for the book itself, I have now read and re-read many chapters of HPMOR: it fully withstands multiple re-readings.

I reread a lot of books, but the only ones I reread immediately after finishing them were the four books of The Book of the New Sun by Gene Wolfe. I literally just put down the fourth book when I finished it and picked up the first and started over.

It's far-future science fiction, though a lot of it feels sort of like fantasy, since it's set in a time when civilization has declined to about the equivalent of bronze age technology. It's also an astonishing work of literature.

The thing is, and the reason I reread it immediately - it's told in the first person, but it's not just a story that happens to be told in the first person. It's actually presented as an autobiography - the real protagonist of the books isn't the character who went here and did this and said that, but the character who's writing a memoir in which he CLAIMS that he went here and did this and said that. And, as is so often the case when people tell stories about themselves, he's not always accurate or honest.

So in order to work out the actual story (or at least as much of it as you can), you can't just read what he says and take it at face value - you have to work out if he's mistaken or lying, and if so, why - what he's failing to note or hiding and why. And that's how you get real insight into the character - not simply by what he says, but by what he noticeably leaves out, or misinterprets, or misrepresents. So you can't just read the story and get it - you have to essentially assemble the real story by reading between the lines. And even though I had been warned before I started the books that he was an untrustworthy narrator, I still had to read them a second time to really start to sort it all out.

FTA:

Energy costs and chemical byproducts are also a problem. The average mechanical pencil requires 22 grams of oil to make, 10 grams of oil for the plastic and 12 grams in terms of the energy costs. The chemical waste created by the manufacturing process can be difficult to dispose of.

Wood pencils require less energy to manufacture, but don’t last as long as their mechanical cousins. The trees necessary to make the pencils are technically a renewable resource, but how they’re harvested can have a big impact on the environment. The wooden pencils that are best for the environment are those that are made out of recycled material or with wood from lumber companies that try to minimize the impact of logging on the eco-system.

I am split on the environmental issue, but I personally think there are different kinds of pencils for different purposes; wooden pencils seem more casual and carefree, like for elementary school, sketching and doodling, whereas mechanical pencils have a more serious sense of purpose about them, like they are used for architectural projects and drafting blueprints and schematic diagrams.
